# Wood Stove

## Setup

I load the firebox top down: a few crumpled sheets of newspaper, a handful of fine kindling, then three small split logs laid across the top so the flames work down through the pile. The flue damper stays fully open until the chimney is drawing hard, and I warm the pipe with a heat gun on cold mornings before I light anything, ten seconds up the flue to reverse the cold air. The first burns of the season stay small while the bricks heat through. I stand with the door cracked and watch for smoke spillage; if any curls into the room, the draw is weak and I need more warmth in the chimney. Once it is going I close the primary air a third of the way and let the secondary burn do the work.

## Maintenance

The flue gets swept in autumn, before the first real fire, and I check the baffle plate at the same time. The door gasket is replaced every two seasons because it hardens and stops sealing, letting air past the glass. I keep 1.5 m clearance to the nearest sofa and curtains, measured from the front face. The glass gets cleaned with a damp cloth and a dip of ash when it clouds over. I keep a spare gasket on the shelf so a failed seal never means a cold week. The ash pan gets emptied into a metal bucket, never a plastic bin where a live ember could sit.

## Notes

Ash goes on the beds outside. A magnetic thermometer on the pipe tells me more than the dial on the front, which lags badly. Damaged firebricks get swapped before they crack through. I keep a week of split logs under cover by the back door so nothing comes in wet.
